corrected_value.title: The Influence of Product Anthropomorphism on Comparative Judgment
corrected_value.title_o: The Influence of Product Anthropomorphism on Comparative Judgment

decisions.quote:
In the fifth installment of
Data Replicada
, we report our attempt to replicate a recently published
Journal of Consumer Research
(JCR) article entitled, “The Influence of Product Anthropomorphism on Comparative Choice” (
.html
).
A product becomes “anthropomorphized” when it is imbued with human-like features, such as a face or a name. For example, this camera, which was presented in this article’s Study 1B, is anthropomorphized:
The article begins with the premise that “people usually form an integrated impression of [an] entire person rather than seeing this person as consisting of separate traits.” The authors then propose that human-like
products
will also be judged in this way: Consumers will be more likely to use a holistic process (vs. an attribute-by-attribute comparison) to judge anthropomorphized products.
This JCR paper contains six studies. We chose to replicate Study 2 (N = 101) because it was the only study run on MTurk.
decisions.reason: The report re-tests only one original study (blind target_index 0): Study 2 (N = 101, MTurk) of a recently published six-study Journal of Consumer Research article on product anthropomorphism and holistic comparative judgment/choice (with Study 1B featuring an anthropomorphized camera and Study 2 comparing two laptops across three star-rated dimensions, originally conducted in early 2015). Automated pairing was left unresolved only because the blog post text rendered the final title word as 'Choice' instead of 'Judgment' (while using 'Judgments' in the post title and 'judge' in the premise summary) and placed the full citation behind the '.html' hyperlink stripped by text extraction. The single tested JCR article matches the shipped original identity.

decisions.quote:
One conclusion could be that the original effect does not truly exist, and the original finding was a false positive. Our evidence is consistent with that. Our evidence is also consistent with the possibility that the original effect might exist but is considerably smaller than what was found in the original. Indeed, combining the p-values of these two replications generates a marginally significant overall effect (p = .071). Nevertheless, it is important to highlight two things. First, any real effect could exist because of the aforementioned confounds. Second, our results imply that the original study was underpowered to around 8%, indicating that its sample size was simply not large enough to detect the effects that we have observed. Indeed, instead of needing 101 participants in the original study, our investigation suggests you’d need at least 3,400.
Conclusion
In sum, using 5.5 times the sample size as the original study, we do not find significant evidence that adorning laptops with human-like features makes consumers more likely to choose the one that has more total stars (instead of the one that is better on more dimensions).
decisions.reason: With the tested original identity resolved to the single JCR article re-tested in this report (target_index 0), both the MTurk (N = 562, d = .09) and Prolific (N = 584, d = .10) replications yielded nonsignificant results, and the replication authors' explicit overall conclusion is that using 5.5 times the original sample size they do not find significant evidence for the original central effect. Both shipped and blind coding agree on 'failed'.

The authors collected new data across two independent online samples (N = 562 on MTurk and N = 584 on Prolific Academic) using the original Qualtrics survey to re-test Study 2 of the published JCR article, making this a replication.
